title: CBDT Brings Relief: No More Arrests for Tax Default, Extended Deadlines for Valuers & Practitioners!
content:
# CBDT Brings Relief: No More Arrests for Tax Default, Extended Deadlines for Valuers & Practitioners!

As tax professionals, we often find ourselves navigating a labyrinth of regulations, amendments, and ever-evolving compliance requirements. The constant pressure of deadlines and the occasional fear of stringent recovery measures can, at times, feel overwhelming. But every now and then, the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) introduces changes that genuinely ease the compliance burden and foster a more trust-based tax environment. One such significant development is the **Income-tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026**, notified on September 17, 2026. This notification brings a sigh of relief on two major fronts: it removes the much-debated arrest provisions for tax recovery and extends crucial deadlines for valuers and authorized income-tax practitioners. *Kya baat hai, this is a welcome move indeed!*

Let's delve deeper into what these amendments entail and their practical implications for us and our clients.

## A Progressive Shift: Decriminalizing Tax Recovery

Perhaps the most impactful change ushered in by these amendments is the removal of provisions related to arrest and detention from the prescribed modes of tax recovery under the Income-tax Rules, 2026. For years, the specter of arrest for tax default, however rarely used, was a point of contention and concern among taxpayers and professionals alike. This fear factor, frankly, often overshadowed the true spirit of cooperative compliance.

The CBDT has now, through the Income-tax (Fourth Amendment) Rules, 2026, significantly amended **Rule 225** of the Income-tax Rules, 2026. Specifically, clause (c) of sub-rule (4) of Rule 225 has been omitted. Furthermore, several sub-rules (namely, 75 to 83 and 91) which detailed the procedures for arrest, detention, and civil imprisonment of tax defaulters, including inquiry, custody, release, and subsistence allowance, have been entirely deleted. The consequential removal of the words "(except arrest and detention)" from sub-rule (87) further solidifies this progressive stance.

This is a monumental shift. It aligns the Income-tax Rules with the broader policy direction indicated in the **Finance Act, 226**, and the **Budget 2026-27** announcements aimed at decriminalizing technical defaults and fostering an environment of greater trust. The intention is clear: tax recovery will continue, *no doubt*, through attachment and sale of movable and immovable property and other asset-based recovery mechanisms, but personal arrest will no longer be a part of the prescribed recovery process under these specific Rules.

It’s important to note, my friends, that these changes to Rules 2 to 4, including the revised Rule 225, are retrospective, having come into force from **April 1, 2026**. This retrospective application is a welcome relief, ensuring that no action could be taken under the now-omitted provisions from the beginning of the current financial year. However, do remember, this amendment specifically deals with the *Rules*; it does not, by itself, extinguish any separate power of arrest that might still exist under the broader framework of the Income-tax Act, 2025. But for practical purposes, this is a huge step forward!

## Extended Deadlines: A Much-Needed Breather for Professionals

In another practical and positive move, the CBDT has extended crucial deadlines for two vital categories of professionals: **Registered Valuers** and **Authorised Income-tax Practitioners**. Many professionals were grappling with the September 30, 2026 deadline for transitioning to the new framework under the Income-tax Act, 2025. Recognizing the ground realities and perhaps the administrative load, the Board has provided a much-needed extension.

The deadline for existing valuers who were registered under the **Wealth-tax Act, 1957**, to update their details and continue their registration as valuers under Section 514 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (as per **Rule 246(4)**), has been extended. The new deadline is now **March 31, 2027**, pushed back from the earlier September 30, 2026. Similarly, the deadline under **Rule 256(4)**, which pertains to the registration of authorised income-tax practitioners, has also been extended to **March 31, 2027**, from September 30, 2026.

This extension grants these professionals an additional six months to complete the necessary formalities and transition smoothly into the new regime. It demonstrates the CBDT’s understanding of the complexities involved in such transitions, especially with the introduction of new application forms.

### Revised Application Forms: Form 169 and Form 171

Accompanying these deadline extensions, the CBDT has also revised the prescribed application forms. **Form 169** is for individuals applying for registration as valuers under Section 514, and **Form 171** is for those seeking registration as authorised income-tax practitioners under Section 515 of the Income-tax Act, 2025.

The revised Form 169 for valuers now requires more comprehensive disclosures. Applicants must furnish detailed personal information, asset class for which they seek registration, educational and professional qualifications, and extensive valuation experience, including work carried out in the preceding three years. A registration fee of ₹10,000 is prescribed, though valuers already registered under the Wealth-tax Act, 1957, are exempt from this fee. Form 171 for income-tax practitioners similarly requires detailed personal and professional particulars.

These changes, including the revised forms and extended deadlines, apply with effect from **September 17, 2026**.

### Other Procedural Refinements

The amendments also include some technical and procedural adjustments:

*   **Rule 160:** A technical correction has been made in Rule 160, replacing the reference "(i)" with "(a)" in sub-rules (3) and (4) to ensure consistency in the rule structure.
*   **Rule 176:** This rule, dealing with faceless assessment proceedings, has been amended. The requirement of "affixing digital signature" for authenticating electronic records by assessment, verification, technical, and review units has been replaced with the broader term "by way of an electronic communication". This reflects a technology-neutral approach to digital interactions within the faceless assessment framework.

## Old vs. New Provisions: A Quick Look

To make things clearer, here’s a snapshot of the key amendments:

| Feature                     | Old Provision (Before Sep 17, 2026)                                                                                                    | New Provision (After Sep 17, 2026)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| :-------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Arrest for Tax Recovery** | Rule 225(4)(c) permitted recovery through arrest and detention; specific sub-rules (75-83, 91) detailed arrest and detention procedures. | **Arrest and detention provisions removed from Rule 225.** Clause (c) of sub-rule (4) omitted, and sub-rules (75) to (83) and (91) deleted. Words "(except arrest and detention)" removed from sub-rule (87). (Retrospective from April 1, 2026).                        |
| **Valuers Registration Deadline** | Existing valuers (under Wealth-tax Act, 1957) to update registration under Rule 246(4) by **September 30, 2026**. | Deadline extended to **March 31, 2027**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Tax Practitioners Registration Deadline** | Authorised Income-tax Practitioners to register under Rule 256(4) by **September 30, 2026**.                       | Deadline extended to **March 31, 2027**.                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Valuer Application Form** | Older Form 169 with existing disclosure requirements.                                                                                  | **Revised Form 169** introduced, requiring more granular details on qualifications, professional history, and valuation experience, including a declaration about disqualification.                                                                                   |
| **Tax Practitioner Application Form** | Older Form 171 with existing disclosure requirements.                                                                                  | **Revised Form 171** introduced, requiring updated personal and professional details.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Authentication in Faceless Assessment (Rule 176)** | Electronic records authenticated "by affixing digital signature".                                                                 | Electronic records authenticated "by way of an electronic communication".                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

## Concluding Thoughts

These amendments by the CBDT are a clear indication of a more nuanced and taxpayer-friendly approach to tax administration. The removal of arrest provisions for tax recovery is a significant move towards building trust and reducing compliance anxieties, focusing on asset-based recovery instead of personal liberty. The extended deadlines for valuers and tax practitioners provide much-needed breathing room, acknowledging the practical challenges involved in adapting to new regulatory frameworks.

As professionals, it's incumbent upon us to understand these changes thoroughly and guide our clients accordingly. These amendments, while seemingly procedural, have far-reaching implications for the ease of doing business and the overall tax climate in India. *Yeh changes toh ekdum mast hain, let's make the most of them!*
